section.title: Introduction
section.para: Text can include encoded files: web pages inline images as data: URIs, documents paste base64 payloads, mail wraps MIME bodies, and logs contain PEM envelopes and JSON Web Tokens. The package opennlp.tools.assets finds such assets as exact spans over the original text, identifies their format, and can replace them with text while keeping every offset mapped to the source.

CursorAssetDetector checks encoded prefixes, validates the payload alphabet and padding, and decodes up to 24 leading bytes for format detection. Bare runs need at least 32 encoded characters and a recognized file signature. The signature table is derived from Apache Tika's media-type catalog. Recognized PNG and GIF headers also provide image dimensions. A declared media type alone does not provide dimensions. Both dimensions are -1 when either is missing or invalid. PNG dimensions require a leading 13-byte IHDR chunk and positive values no greater than 2,147,483,647. GIF dimensions describe the logical screen. A signature match does not establish that a file is complete, valid, or safe to open.
XAR archives are reported as xar with media type application/x-xar, not Xara graphics. Encoded XPM images are reported as xpm with media type image/x-xpixmap.

Explicitly typed, base64 data: URIs accept non-empty payloads, including one- and two-byte values. The media type retains parameters such as charset=UTF-8; the format name excludes them. Non-base64 data URIs and percent-encoded payload characters are not supported.

Malformed padding, mixed standard and URL-safe alphabets, and line-wrapped URL-safe payloads are rejected. For an unpadded run with length 1 modulo 4, the scanner omits the final character to recover a decodable prefix. This recovery does not repair or validate the underlying file.

section.title: Detecting and decoding
Wrapped base64, PEM, and JWT
section.para: Bare standard-base64 payloads can cross LF or CRLF line separators when their continued lines use the conventional 76-column MIME or 64-column PEM width. The final line may be shorter. Unwrapped payloads may instead use the URL-safe alphabet from RFC 4648 section 5. The detector still requires a known and decoded file magic before it reports either form as a bare asset.

A textual envelope following RFC 7468 is different: its verified, matching BEGIN and END labels identify the content. The asset span covers the full envelope while the payload span covers only its line-wrapped body, so decode returns the DER bytes directly. Empty bodies, mismatched labels, lines longer than 64 characters, invalid padding, and non-base64 body characters fail closed.

section.title: Folding assets into text
section.para:
AssetAnnotator provides the opennlp:assets layer, and AssetFolder replaces every asset with text. The result is an AlignedText: spans over the folded text map back to exact original offsets, so downstream findings over the cleaned text still locate in the raw input. The default replacement renders a caption from the asset's own metadata:
Document document = new AssetAnnotator().annotate(Document.of(text)); AlignedText folded = AssetFolder.fold(document, AssetFolder.caption()); // folded.normalizedString() = "An image [png 5x7, 45 bytes] follows."
Mapping the caption back recovers the asset's exact span in the original: folded.toOriginalSpan(9, 28), the caption's offsets in the folded text, returns the span of the whole data URI.

What replaces an asset is the caller's choice through the replacement function. A BinaryContentDescriber can extract document text or generate an image description:
BinaryContentDescriber describer = ...; // supplied by the caller
AlignedText described = AssetFolder.fold(document, annotation -> describer.describe(annotation.value().decode(text), annotation.value().mediaType()));
The interface takes bytes and a media type and returns text. OpenNLP ships no implementation. Applications provide the extraction or captioning service.
